lessons.title: Files & directories: ls, cd, pwd, mkdir, cp, mv, rm
objectives: Navigate and manage files and directories from the command line
Explain how ls changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect ls with cd and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Linux files and directories form a hierarchical filesystem. `pwd` shows your current directory, `ls` lists its contents, and commands such as `cd`, `mkdir`, `cp`, `mv`, and `rm` let you navigate and manage files. The key is understanding relative and absolute paths so you know exactly which location a command will affect.
examples:
pwd                    # /home/user
ls
cd ..
mkdir new_folder
cp source.txt dest.txt
mv old_name.txt new_name.txt
rm -r old_folder
commonMistakes: Running rm -r on the wrong directory -- there's no recycle bin by default, so double-check the path before pressing enter.
lessons.careerRelevance: These core navigation commands are used constantly in any real terminal-based workflow.

lessons.title: Absolute vs relative paths, and `~`
objectives: Distinguish absolute from relative paths
Explain how absolute path changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect absolute path with relative path and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An absolute path starts from the root directory / and fully specifies a location regardless of where you currently are. A relative path is interpreted relative to your current working directory.
examples:
cd /home/user/projects   # absolute -- works from anywhere
cd projects                # relative -- only works if you're already in /home/user
cd ~                       # jumps to your home directory
commonMistakes: Using a relative path in a script that might run from a different working directory -- it silently looks in the wrong place.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding path types prevents a very common class of 'file not found' confusion.

lessons.title: Viewing & searching file contents
objectives: Use cat, head, tail, grep, and find
Explain how cat changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect cat with head and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: cat prints a file's entire contents. head shows the first lines (head -n 5 for the first 5); tail shows the last, and tail -f keeps watching for new lines appended in real time -- useful for live log files.
examples:
cat file.txt
head -n 5 file.txt
tail -f server.log
grep "error" server.log
find . -name "*.py"
commonMistakes: Using cat on a huge file when you only need the first or last few lines -- head/tail are faster and don't flood your terminal.
lessons.careerRelevance: These are the everyday tools for inspecting logs and source files on any real server or dev machine.

lessons.title: Redirection & pipes in depth
objectives: Redirect output to files and chain commands together with pipes
Explain how redirect > changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect redirect > with >> and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: > writes a command's output to a file, overwriting anything already there. >> appends instead of overwriting.
examples:
echo "hello" > out.txt       # overwrites out.txt
echo "again" >> out.txt      # appends to out.txt
cat log.txt | grep "error"   # pipes cat's output into grep
commonMistakes: Using > when you meant >> -- this silently overwrites and destroys the file's previous contents.
lessons.careerRelevance: Pipes and redirection are core Unix philosophy: small tools combined flexibly, rather than one giant program doing everything.

lessons.title: Permissions & sudo
objectives: Change file permissions and run commands with elevated privileges
Explain how chmod changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect chmod with chmod +x and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: chmod +x script.sh makes a file executable. sudo runs a single command with elevated (administrator) privileges -- necessary for actions a regular user account isn't allowed to do, like installing system-wide software.
examples:
chmod +x deploy.sh
./deploy.sh
sudo apt install some-package
commonMistakes: Using sudo by default for everything 'just in case' -- elevated privileges should be reserved for when they're actually needed, to avoid accidental system-wide damage.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding permissions and when sudo is genuinely necessary is a real security-relevant skill.

lessons.title: Shell Scripting Basics
objectives: Write a basic bash script with variables, conditionals, and a loop, and understand why the shebang line matters
Explain how shebang changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect shebang with #!/bin/bash and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A shell script is just a text file of commands you'd otherwise type one by one, run as a program -- the first line, `#!/bin/bash` (the shebang), tells the system which interpreter should run it. Variables are set with `NAME=value` (no spaces around `=`) and read with `$NAME`; `$1`, `$2` etc.
examples:
#!/bin/bash
# backup.sh -- takes a folder name as its one argument
FOLDER=$1
if [ -d "$FOLDER" ]; then
  tar -czf "${FOLDER}_$(date +%Y-%m-%d).tar.gz" "$FOLDER"
  echo "Backed up $FOLDER"
else
  echo "Error: $FOLDER not found" >&2
  exit 1
fi
commonMistakes: Forgetting to make a script executable (chmod +x) before trying to run it directly, or putting spaces around `=` when setting a variable (`NAME = value` is a syntax error in bash, unlike.
lessons.careerRelevance: Writing a small, correct bash script to automate a repetitive task is a routine, practical expectation in almost any backend or infrastructure-adjacent role.
lessons.explain: A shell script is just a text file of commands you'd otherwise type one by one, run as a program -- the first line, `#!/bin/bash` (the shebang), tells the system which interpreter should run it. lessons.title: Environment Variables & Package Management
objectives: Use environment variables (including PATH) correctly, and install/manage software with a package manager
Explain how environment variable changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect environment variable with export and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An environment variable (set with `export NAME=value`) is available to any program launched from that shell -- PATH is the most important one: a list of directories the shell searches, in order, when you type a command name, which is why 'command not found' often means the program either isn't installed or isn't in a directory PATH includes.
examples:
export API_KEY="abc123"        # available to programs launched from this shell
echo $PATH                     # colon-separated list of directories searched for commands

sudo apt update && sudo apt install nginx   # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo dnf install nginx                       # RHEL/Fedora
brew install nginx                           # macOS
commonMistakes: Assuming 'command not found' always means the software isn't installed -- it often means it IS installed, just not in a directory listed in PATH, which is a different problem with a.
lessons.careerRelevance: Diagnosing PATH issues and comfortably using a package manager are routine, near-daily practical skills once you're working on a real Linux server, not just a local dev machine.

lessons.title: Networking & Remote Access: curl, SSH & scp
objectives: Connect to a remote server over SSH and use curl/scp to interact with it
Explain how SSH changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SSH with ssh key and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell) lets you log into and run commands on a remote machine over an encrypted connection -- `ssh user@host` opens a remote shell session, and SSH keys (a public/private key pair) let you authenticate without typing a password every time, which is both more convenient and more secure than password auth.
examples:
ssh ahmed@my-server.example.com          # open a remote shell session
scp local-file.txt ahmed@my-server:/home/ahmed/   # copy a file TO the server
scp ahmed@my-server:/var/log/app.log .            # copy a file FROM the server

curl https://api.example.com/health      # quick check: is this endpoint responding?
curl -X POST -d '{"key":"value"}' https://api.example.com/data
commonMistakes: Relying on password authentication for SSH instead of setting up key-based auth -- beyond being less convenient, password auth over SSH is a much more common target for automated brute-force.
lessons.careerRelevance: SSH, scp, and curl are used constantly and directly in real day-to-day backend and infrastructure work -- connecting to servers, moving files, and checking whether a deployed service is actually responding.
lessons.explain: SSH (Secure Shell) lets you log into and run commands on a remote machine over an encrypted connection -- `ssh user@host` opens a remote shell session, and SSH keys (a public/private key pair) let you authenticate without typing a password every time, which is both more convenient and more secure than password auth.

description: The environment real engineering happens in.

interviewPreparation.q: A command works when you type it directly but fails when run from a script or cron job. What would you check?
interviewPreparation.a: Whether PATH is set up the same way in that context -- scripts and cron jobs often run with a much more limited PATH than your interactive shell, so a command that resolves fine when you type it can fail with 'command not found' in a script unless it's referenced with its full path or PATH is set explicitly.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is key-based SSH authentication preferred over password authentication?
interviewPreparation.a: It's both more convenient (no password prompt every connection) and more secure -- password authentication over SSH is a much more common target for automated brute-force attempts, while key-based auth requires possessing the actual private key, which is far harder to guess or brute-force.

interviewPreparation.q: What does a script's exit code communicate, and why does it matter beyond just 'did it crash'?
interviewPreparation.a: Exit code 0 means success, nonzero means failure -- and other scripts, CI pipelines, and tools rely on this to decide what to do next (like whether to proceed to the next step or stop). A script that always exits 0 even when something went wrong will silently let failures pass through undetected by anything checking its exit code.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you diagnose a 'command not found' error right after installing something with a package manager?
interviewPreparation.a: First confirm the package manager actually believes it's installed (its own query/list command), then check whether the installed binary's location is actually in PATH -- a genuinely failed install and a PATH problem look identical from the error message alone but need different fixes.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between curl and a full script for checking whether a service is healthy?
interviewPreparation.a: curl is fast for a one-off manual check -- hit an endpoint, see the response, done. A script is worth it when you need this repeated automatically, combined with other logic (alerting, logging, retries), or run on a schedule -- curl alone doesn't decide what to do with the result, a script does.

capstone.title: Automate a real task with a script, deployed and run on a remote server
capstone.description: Write a genuinely useful bash script (not a toy example) that automates something real -- log analysis, a backup routine, a health check -- then actually deploy and run it on a remote server you connect to over SSH, using a package manager to install anything it needs there. This capstone is about practical Linux fluency under real conditions: a script that only works on your machine, in your exact environment, isn't actually done.
deliverables: A bash script with real logic (variables, at least one conditional, at least one loop) solving an actual problem, not a 'hello world' demo
The script made executable and run successfully, with its exit code checked and used correctly (nonzero on failure)
SSH access set up to a remote server (key-based, not password), with the script copied over via scp and run there
Any dependency the script needs installed on the remote server via a package manager -- not assumed to already be present
A short written note on one thing that behaved differently on the remote server than locally, and how you diagnosed it
capstone.portfolioTips: The note about something that broke on the remote server and how you fixed it is the most convincing part -- it's concrete evidence you've actually operated on a real server, not just written a script that happens to run in one specific environment.

industryUsage.usage: Bash/shell scripting for everyday automation and SSH-based remote server work are baseline, constantly-used skills across nearly every backend and infrastructure role, not specialized knowledge.

Operating real Linux servers (via SSH, package management, and shell scripting for automation) underlies most of AWS's own infrastructure and is assumed fluency for engineers working close to production systems.
Given its scale, automating repetitive operational tasks with shell scripts (log analysis, health checks, backups) is routine, practical daily work, not an advanced or optional skill.
